explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. David swears, “I will not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids…” (Psalm 132:4). He names his eyes AND his eyelids, like he's covering every angle. I would last about four minutes before my chef's hat slid down over my face.

Food isn't on David's list, friend. The oath names his house, his bed, and then sleep for his eyes and eyelids. An oath this big sounds like it should come with skipped meals, but the song never says that, so I'm not adding it. Sleep is the one that's in the verse.

No visitors in this oath, baker. David's list is his house, his bed, and sleep for his eyes and eyelids (Psalm 132:3-4). Nobody on that list is a guest. I'm picturing a neighbor knocking and David just waving from the yard, but that's me, not the song.

That's it, friend. David swears he won't rest “until I find a place for the LORD, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob.” Look at what he's hunting for: a dwelling for the LORD, and nothing about a nicer place for himself. That's an oath with the focus in the right spot.

explanations.answer: A way to beat his enemies
explanations.explanation: Enemies aren't part of David's oath, baker. He swears he won't rest until he finds “a place for the LORD, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob” (Psalm 132:5). Enemies do show up at the very end of the song, in the LORD's own words in verse 18. In David's oath, though, the whole mission is a dwelling.

The throne comes up later, friend, and it's the LORD doing the promising, not David. Here in David's oath, the thing he's searching for is “a place for the LORD, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob.” The promise about his throne arrives in verse 11. Easy to mix up two oaths in one song!

Yes, baker. The group says, “Let us go to His dwelling place; let us worship at His footstool.” They're not just saying it to the air. They're inviting each other, which I love, because worship is better with company. Even bakers who work alone like me end up with a crowd around the cookie box eventually.

Close to a good idea, friend, but guarding isn't in the verse. The group says, “Let us go to His dwelling place; let us worship at His footstool.” The invitation is to worship, nothing about posting up at the door. I think a footstool sounds like a place to bow down, not to stand watch.

The vow was David's, baker, back in verses 2 through 5. This group is doing something different. They say, “Let us go to His dwelling place; let us worship at His footstool.” One person swears an oath, and then a whole crowd shows up to worship.
That's the one, baker. The song says, “Arise, O LORD, to Your resting place, You and the ark of Your strength.” Strength and rest in the same sentence. I like a sentence that can hold both.

I see why you went there, friend. “The ark of Your strength” sounds like it's marching off to something big. But the verse asks Him to arise “to Your resting place,” and there's no battlefield in it. Strength is in the verse, but the destination is rest.

No city gates in this verse, baker. The song says, “Arise, O LORD, to Your resting place, You and the ark of Your strength.” That's the whole destination. The gates just didn't make the song this time.
It's actually False, baker. The song says the opposite: “…and Your saints shout for joy” (Psalm 132:9). Shouting, not weeping. That's a whole different volume and a whole different mood.

Right, baker. The verse says, “May Your priests be clothed with righteousness, and Your saints shout for joy.” The song asks for joy, not tears. The only thing getting shouted in this verse is happiness, and I'd be shouting too.

Yes, friend. The song says, “For the sake of Your servant David, do not reject Your anointed one.” It's a plain request, and it's tied to David's name. Two short lines, and they carry a whole lot of asking.

Testing isn't what the song asks about, baker. The request is, “For the sake of Your servant David, do not reject Your anointed one” (Psalm 132:10). The word is reject. Nothing in that line is about tests, so you can put your pencil down.

Not humble, friend. Verse 10 asks, “For the sake of Your servant David, do not reject Your anointed one.” The word that sits there is reject, plain and simple. The song doesn't use humble anywhere in this line.

That's right, baker. The song says, “The LORD swore an oath to David, a promise He will not revoke: ‘One of your descendants I will place on your throne.’” Notice the phrase, a promise He will not revoke. That's about as solid as a promise gets.

Priests are in this song, friend, but not on the throne. The LORD's promise is, “One of your descendants I will place on your throne” (Psalm 132:11). Priests show up in verse 9 and verse 16, getting clothed. The throne belongs to David's descendants.

No mighty men in this promise, baker. The LORD says, “One of your descendants I will place on your throne” (Psalm 132:11). The promise is about family, not an army. Nobody in the song gets a mighty-man title here.

explanations.answer: Their sons will sit on his throne forever
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says, “If your sons keep My covenant and the testimony I will teach them, then their sons will also sit on your throne forever and ever.” The if is real, and so is the promise that follows it. The reward goes past David's sons all the way to their sons.

explanations.answer: Their names will be great in all the earth
explanations.explanation: That sounds nice, friend, but it's not in the verse. The LORD says, “then their sons will also sit on your throne forever and ever” (Psalm 132:12). The reward is about the throne and the next generation. Great names don't come up.

explanations.answer: Their enemies will bow down at their feet
explanations.explanation: Enemies aren't in this promise, baker. The LORD says, “then their sons will also sit on your throne forever and ever” (Psalm 132:12). The only time enemies come up in this song is verse 18, and there they're clothed with shame. Here the promise is sons, and their sons, on the throne.

That's it, baker. The song says, “For the LORD has chosen Zion; He has desired it for His home.” Chosen and desired, two warm words in one line. A home is something you want, not just something you end up with.

No battle camp in this verse, friend. The song says the LORD “has chosen Zion; He has desired it for His home” (Psalm 132:13). A camp is a place you pass through, but a home is where you settle in. The verse uses the word home.

Storehouse isn't the word, baker. The LORD has chosen Zion and “has desired it for His home” (Psalm 132:13). I think a storehouse is a place you keep things, and a home is a place somebody lives. The verse goes with home.

It's actually False, baker. The LORD says, “This is My resting place forever and ever; here I will dwell, for I have desired this home.” Forever and ever is nowhere near the length of one lifetime. It's the opposite of a short stay.

Yes, friend. The LORD says, “This is My resting place forever and ever; here I will dwell, for I have desired this home.” Forever and ever doesn't stop when David's life does. The time limit in the statement just isn't in the verse.
Yes, baker. The LORD says, “I will satisfy her poor with bread.” Satisfy is a good word, because it means more than just getting by. Bread is the one food in this line, so I'll leave it right there.
Not kings, friend. The LORD says, “I will satisfy her poor with bread” (Psalm 132:15). The ones who get satisfied are the poor. Kings are nowhere in that line.
Soldiers don't show up in this verse, baker. The LORD says, “I will satisfy her poor with bread” (Psalm 132:15). The word that fits the blank is poor. The bread is for them.

Yes, baker. The song asked, “May Your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Psalm 132:9), and the LORD says, “I will clothe her priests with salvation” (Psalm 132:16). Same clothing word, different outfit. I do enjoy a good wardrobe change.

It's actually True, friend. The LORD says, “I will clothe her priests with salvation” (Psalm 132:16). Earlier the song asked for righteousness (Psalm 132:9), and here the LORD speaks of salvation. It's the same clothing word both times.
That's right, baker. The LORD says, “I have prepared a lamp for My anointed one.” Prepared is the word that caught my ear. I know a little about getting something ready ahead of time.
No sword here, friend. The LORD says, “I have prepared a lamp for My anointed one” (Psalm 132:17). The thing He prepared is a lamp. Not every strong line needs a weapon in it.

Robes are a good guess, baker, since this song has a lot of clothing in it. But for the anointed one in verse 17, the LORD says, “I have prepared a lamp for My anointed one.” The clothing in this song goes to the priests and the enemies. The anointed one gets a lamp.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, “I will clothe his enemies with shame, but the crown upon him will gleam.” Shame goes in the first blank. Notice it's another clothing word, so even the enemies get dressed in this song.
Yes, friend. The last line says, “I will clothe his enemies with shame, but the crown upon him will gleam.” Gleam is the word for the crown. That's a nice way for a song to end.

Honor is a lovely word, baker, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says, “I will clothe his enemies with shame, but the crown upon him will gleam.” The enemies get shame, not honor. Honor just didn't make it into the last line.

No breaking in this verse, friend. The last line says, “I will clothe his enemies with shame, but the crown upon him will gleam.” The crown gleams, and nothing about it breaks. I'd rather the crown stay in one piece too, like a cookie out of a good stamp.
Fade isn't the word, baker. The LORD says, “I will clothe his enemies with shame, but the crown upon him will gleam.” The crown gleams, so it's shining, not dimming. The song ends on a bright note.
